The '''Leavenworth Detention Center''' was a privately run maximum-security federal prison located in [[Leavenworth, Kansas]]. The facility is owned and was operated by [[CoreCivic]] formerly named Corrections Corporation of America under contract with the [[United States Marshals Service]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cca.com/facilities/leavenworth-detention-center#|title = CoreCivic: Better the Public Good}}</ref>

The detention center reopened in March 2026 under the new name of '''Midwest Regional Reception Center''', still operated by CoreCivic. In its reopened incarnation, the facility can hold up to 1,033 detained immigrants, and has a staff of 300.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Article |first=Matthew Kelly Gift |date=2026-03-11 |title=ICE detention center can open in Leavenworth after private prison wins long fight |url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article314984556.html |access-date=2026-05-28 |work=Kansas City Star}}</ref> On March 19, 2026, the facility was holding 20 detainees; by May, the population rose to 249.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Motter |first=Sarah |date=2026-03-20 |title=Leavenworth ICE detention facility opens with 20 detainees, days after contentious vote |url=https://www.kctv5.com/2026/03/20/leavenworth-ice-detention-facility-opens-with-20-detainees-days-after-contentious-vote/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |work=KCTV5}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Shackelford-Nwanganga |first=Bek |date=2026-05-06 |title=Leavenworth's for-profit ICE detention center under scrutiny from new community board |url=https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2026-05-06/leavenworths-for-profit-ice-detention-center-under-scrutiny-from-new-community-board |access-date=2026-05-28 |work=KCUR - Kansas City news and NPR}}</ref>

==History==
When originally constructed as a 460-bed [[private prison]], it was the first correctional facility under direct contract with a U.S. federal agency.<ref>{{cite web|last=Leavenworth Convention and Visitor's Bureau|title=Prison city|date=August 7, 2024 |url=http://www.lvarea.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=category&layout=blog&id=26&Itemid=52}}</ref> In May 2008 the facility underwent its fourth expansion to increase capacity to 1,126 inmates.<ref>{{cite web|last=City of Lansing|title=our Partners|url=http://www.lansing.ks.us/index.aspx?NID=244|access-date=2013-07-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202100605/http://www.lansing.ks.us/index.aspx?NID=244|archive-date=2014-02-02|url-status=dead}}</ref> It held both male and female prisoners.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cca.com/facilities/leavenworth-detention-center#|title = CoreCivic: Better the Public Good}}</ref>

A 2017 [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] (DOJ) Office of the Inspector General's report found understaffing and lack of oversight that lead to “issues affecting the safety and security” of the facility.

In January 2021, U.S. President [[Joe Biden]] issued [[Executive Order 14006]], which prevented federal agencies from renewing contracts with privately run prisons.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/01/26/executive-order-reforming-our-incarceration-system-to-eliminate-the-use-of-privately-operated-criminal-detention-facilities/|title = Executive Order on Reforming Our Incarceration System to Eliminate the Use of Privately Operated Criminal Detention Facilities| date=January 26, 2021 }}</ref>

In September 2021, [[American Civil Liberties Union]] (ACLU) affiliates and federal public defender offices in Kansas, Missouri, Iowa, and Nebraska sent a joint letter to the White House Domestic Policy Counsel to immediately close the Core Civic Detention Facility in Leavenworth,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aclukansas.org/sites/default/files/field_documents/letter_regarding_corecivic_leavenworth_redacted.pdf/|title = White House Domestic Policy Counsel Office, Leavenworth Cou. Commission re: Corecivic Leavenworth }}</ref> detailing the numerous reports each office had received about the Leavenworth facility from current and former staff and from residents and their families. CoreCivic's severe understaffing and profit-driven shortcuts ensured that stabbings, suicides, and homicides occurred with alarming frequency. Weapons, drugs, and other contraband were a common occurrence. In addition to all of the violence, CoreCivic neglected basic human needs in its Leavenworth Facility, restricting food, curtailing or cutting off contact with legal counsel and family, limiting medical care and even basic necessities like showers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kmbc.com/article/aclu-push-to-close-private-leavenworth-kansas-prison/37995336|title = ACLU continues push to close private Leavenworth prison| date=October 18, 2021 }}</ref>

The facility's contract was allowed to expire on schedule in December 2021 without renewal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tolan |first=Casey |date=2021-11-12 |title=Biden vowed to close federal private prisons, but prison companies are finding loopholes to keep them open  |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/12/politics/biden-private-prisons-immigration-detention-centers-invs/index.html |access-date=2025-05-17 |website=CNN Politics |language=en}}</ref> The facility has remained inactive.<ref>{{cite web|title=Leavenworth Detention Center|url=https://www.corecivic.com/facilities/leavenworth-detention-center|access-date=2022-10-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220818012546/https://www.corecivic.com/facilities/leavenworth-detention-center|archive-date=2022-08-18}}</ref>

In 2024, records produced in a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit filed by the ACLU against Immigration and Customs Enforcement responded to a request for proposal from ICE revealed that the Leavenworth facility, or Midwest Regional Reception Center, was among the CoreCivic facilities submitted for consideration of a contract.<ref>{{Cite press release|date=2024-12-19 |title=ACLU FOIA Litigation Reveals ICE Actively Considering Proposals to Expand Immigration Detention in Kansas |url=https://www.aclukansas.org/en/press-releases/aclu-foia-litigation-reveals-ice-actively-considering-proposals-expand-immigration |access-date=2025-03-18 |publisher=ACLU of Kansas |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Multi-State Detention Facility Support FOIA Documents - Request for Information |url=https://www.aclu.org/documents/multi-state-detention-facility-support-foia-documents-request-for-information |access-date=2025-03-18 |website=American Civil Liberties Union |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kite |first=Allison |date=2024-12-19 |title=Shuttered private jail in Kansas could become immigration detention center |url=https://kansasreflector.com/2024/12/19/shuttered-private-jail-in-kansas-could-become-immigration-detention-center/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=Kansas Reflector |language=en-US}}</ref>

In February 2025, CoreCivic submitted an application to the City of Leavenworth for a special use permit as required by city ordinance, an explicit statement of its purpose of opening the facility for ICE detentions, and followed up by hosting a private event listed as "an informational luncheon" with “a small number of leaders from the city, county and state level as well as multiple tours of the facility describing their intentions for the space as an ICE detention center.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-02-24 |title=Residents, advocates react to CoreCivic submitting application to city of Leavenworth for ICE detention center |url=https://www.kshb.com/news/local-news/corecivic-submits-application-to-city-of-leavenworth-for-ice-detention-center |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KSHB 41 Kansas City News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Letter to city director of planning {{!}} PDF |publisher=City of Leavenworth |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/832827403/Letter-to-city-director-of-planning |access-date=2025-03-18 |via=Scribd |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=Press Release on CoreCivic Special Use Permit Application |publisher =Leavenworth, Kansas |url=https://www.leavenworthks.org/ru/page/press-release-corecivic-special-use-permit-application |access-date=2025-03-18}}</ref> The proposal received opposition from the ACLU of Kansas, Advocates for Immigrants Rights and Reconciliation, former employees, and local residents<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-02-05 |title=In city already filled with detention centers, potential ICE facility worries Leavenworth residents |url=https://www.kshb.com/news/local-news/in-city-already-filled-with-detention-centers-potential-ice-facility-worries-leavenworth-residents |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KSHB 41 Kansas City News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Webster |first1=Betsy |last2=Brennan |first2=Nathan |date=2025-02-26 |title=A look inside potential ICE detention in Leavenworth |url=https://www.kctv5.com/2025/02/26/city-officials-consider-proposal-ice-detention-facility-leavenworth/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KCTV5 |language=en}}</ref> Weeks later in mid-March, CoreCivic withdrew its application for the permit.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-03-14 |title=CoreCivic withdrawing application for ICE detention center in Leavenworth |url=https://www.kshb.com/news/local-news/corecivic-withdrawing-application-for-ice-detention-center-in-leavenworth |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KSHB 41 Kansas City News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Dailey |first=Greg |date=2025-03-14 |title=CoreCivic withdraws application to open as ICE facility in Leavenworth |url=https://www.kctv5.com/2025/03/14/corecivic-withdraws-application-open-ice-facility-leavenworth/ |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KCTV5 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sloan |first=Nick |date=2025-03-17 |title=CoreCivic withdraws permit application for ICE detention center in Leavenworth |url=https://www.kmbc.com/article/corecivic-withdraws-permit-application-for-ice-detention-center-in-leavenworth/64200556 |access-date=2025-03-18 |work=KMBC |language=en}}</ref> The city then filed suit over CoreCivic's plan to reopen the facility without going through a permitting process.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Chilson |first=Morgan |date=2025-05-16 |title=Leavenworth sues to keep CoreCivic from reopening Kansas prison as ICE detention facility |url=https://www.kake.com/home/leavenworth-sues-to-keep-corecivic-from-reopening-kansas-prison-as-ice-detention-facility/article_ccb43a99-743b-43d6-8de1-059e33b6872a.html |work=KAKE |language=en |agency=Kansas Reflector}}</ref> In March a judge issued a temporary restraining order against CoreCivic opening the facility without a permit from the city.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hollingsworth |first=Heather |date=2025-06-04 |title=Judge blocks private prison operator from housing ICE detainees at shuttered Kansas center |url=https://apnews.com/article/immigrant-detention-leavenworth-6c05f362ff8e9122aea03cb39b4fdebd |access-date=2025-06-05 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

The dispute with city government continued until March 10, 2026, when the Leavenworth City Council approved permission for the prison to operate. Under terms of an agreement with the city, CoreCivic will pay an immediate $1.5 million fee, followed by $400,000 annually to support additional policing and administrative costs.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Kelly |first=Matthew |date=2026-03-11 |title=ICE detention center can open in Leavenworth after private prison wins long fight |url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article314984556.html |access-date=2026-05-28 |work=Kansas City Star}}</ref> The approval came despite protests and years of protest campaigns against the facility.<ref name=":2" /> Detainees began arriving less than two weeks later, with 20 held at the facility on March 19 and 249 by mid-May.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Following its reopening, detainees have reported issues with [[medical neglect]], inadequate food, prolonged [[Lockdown#Prisons|lockdowns]], inability to communicate with legal teams, and staff shortages.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Levey |first=Nathalie |date=2026-09-18 |title=ICE Revives Former “Hellhole” Prison — And Hires the Same Company To Run It |url=https://theintercept.com/2026/09/18/leavenworth-kansas-corecivic-prison-ice-staffing/ |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=The Intercept |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Kelly |first=Matthew |date=August 9, 2026 |title=CoreCivic sells Kansas ICE prison to the feds as activists allege medical neglect |url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article316787550.html |access-date=2026-09-30 |work=The Kansas City Star}}</ref> In August 2026, CoreCivic sold the facility to the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]] for $238.4 million.<ref name=":3" />

==Other area facilities ==

The Leavenworth Detention Center was one of five state, federal and military prisons in the Leavenworth / Lansing area. The other four are:
* [[Lansing Correctional Facility]], operated by the [[Kansas Department of Corrections]]
* [[United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth]] (USP) and its satellite prison camp, operated by the [[Federal Bureau of Prisons]]
* [[United States Disciplinary Barracks]], the [[United States Armed Forces|U.S. military]]'s only [[prison#Security levels|maximum-security]] facility
* [[Midwest Joint Regional Correctional Facility]], another [[United States Armed Forces|U.S. military]] facility
